record.paper_title: FPT Suspects and Tough Customers: Open Problems of Downey and Fellows
record.original_question: Given k sequences Xi over a fixed alphabet Σ and a positive integer m, is there a string X in Σ* of length m that is a subsequence of every Xi?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Fix a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ and consider $\Sigma^*$, the set of finite strings over $\Sigma$. A string $Y = y_1 y_2 \cdots y_m \in \Sigma^*$ is a subsequence of a string $Z = z_1 z_2 \cdots z_n \in \Sigma^*$ if there exist indices $1 \le i_1 < i_2 < \cdots < i_m \le n$ with $z_{i_j} = y_j$ for all $j$.

Define the parameterized decision problem Fixed-Alphabet Longest Common Subsequence as follows.
- Instance: An integer $k \ge 1$, sequences $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_k \in \Sigma^*$, and a positive integer $m$.
- Parameter: $k$ (the number of sequences); the alphabet $\Sigma$ is fixed (independent of the input).
- Question: Does there exist $X \in \Sigma^*$ with $|X| = m$ such that $X$ is a subsequence of $X_i$ for every $i \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$?

Determine the parameterized complexity of this problem with respect to the parameter $k$. In particular, decide whether it is fixed-parameter tractable, or alternatively establish hardness for some level of the W-hierarchy.
artifact.status_search_result: Krzysztof Pietrzak (J. Comput. System Sci. 67 (2003), 757–771) proved that Fixed-Alphabet Longest Common Subsequence, parameterized by the number k of input sequences, is W[1]-hard, ruling out an FPT algorithm of the form f(k)·n^O(1) unless FPT = W[1]. This resolves the parameterized-complexity status posed in the problem.

status_evidence.title: On the parameterized complexity of the fixed alphabet shortest common supersequence and longest common subsequence problems
status_evidence.snippet: Pietrzak shows the Fixed Alphabet LCS and SCS problems parameterized by the number of strings are W[1]-hard.
status_evidence.claim: Fixed-Alphabet LCS parameterized by k is W[1]-hard.

status_evidence.title: Pietrzak — ETH Crypto Group publication page
status_evidence.snippet: Shows W[1]-hardness of Fixed Alphabet LCS and SCS, ruling out f(k)n^c algorithms unless W[1]=FPT.
status_evidence.claim: No FPT algorithm exists for Fixed-Alphabet LCS in parameter k unless FPT=W[1].
